catalog_quote: Mead 1998:92: 'The first major split to occur in the post Proto-Bungku-Tolaki (PBT) period was a breakup into eastern and western branches. The former is represented today principally by Moronene, Kulisusu, Wawonii, Bungku and Mori Bawah; the latter by Padoe, Mori Atas, and Tolaki.' Mead 1998:96-97 (sec. 3.1.2 Syllable patterns and stress): 'The syllable patterns reconstructed for Proto-Bungku-Tolaki are V(C) and CV(C), with a coda possible only in word-final position ... I assume that in Proto-Bungku-Tolaki stress fell on the penultimate syllable, there being no reason to reconstruct otherwise. All present-day Bungku-Tolaki languages also exhibit penultimate stress.' Mead 1999:101-102 (Appendix 3, Selected word lists, incl. Wawonii): '(g) In the absence of any stress marking, one can assume penultimate stress occurring on the next to last written vowel. ... audit.reasoning: Quote check: the deciding sentence (Mead 1998:97) is verbatim on the page image we hold and scanned; the supporting loci (Mead 1998:92 naming Wawonii; Mead 1999:101-102 convention (g), note (d), V/CV syllables) are verbatim in the PL D-91 text we hold layer. Deciding source: a comparative-historical PhD dissertation (1998) plus its Pacific Linguistics condensation (1999) by the field's Bungku-Tolaki specialist, who collected the Wawonii/Menui word lists himself -- first-hand but a family-level blanket statement, not a Wawonii phonology; no discussion of domain, clitics or secondary stress (record correctly codes domain not stated by the source, exceptions none-stated). Better sources: Glottolog lists only two Pusat Bahasa sketches; the one we hold (Hente et al. 1995, Menui dialect) has a complete phonology chapter with no stress statement; the other (Manyambeang et al. 1982/83, 134 pp) is unheld and print-only. A

sources.quote: No statement of stress position. Confirms five vowels, (C)V-dominant syllable structure, identical-vowel sequences pronounced as two syllables (hiatus) rather than long vowels -- consistent with Mead 1999 (d).
sources.locator: whole paper read via text layer; only stress mentions are generic (p. 153 'implications for syllable count, stress patterns'; p. 156 'each vowel maintains relatively equal stress')

sources.note: The only Wawonii-proper description in Glottolog; Pusat Bahasa 'Struktur' sketches have a Fonologi chapter that often includes a 'tekanan' (stress) note. Our classification rests on a family-wide one-liner (Mead 1998:97); this could supply a Wawonii-specific statement and any clitic/suffix behaviour.
